title: Can Milburn rise to the scale of Britain’s NEETs challenge?
gist: Resolution Foundation sets out a five-test framework for judging the Milburn Review of Britain's ~1 million NEET 18–24-year-olds: the UK's gap versus peers is an education-participation problem, not an employment one, and the fix requires FE funding, ringfencing the apprenticeship levy for under-25s, targeted job subsidies over NI tax cuts, mandatory 'career start' support, and several £bn of new money that benefit cuts alone cannot fund.

themes.theme: UK NEET gap is an education deficit, not a jobs deficit

insights.claim: Around one million 18–24-year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training (NEET), and they are a heterogeneous group differing in job search, benefit receipt, health and duration of NEET status.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Scale of youth inactivity is a structural drag on UK labour supply and potential growth; policy must be segmented rather than one-size.
insights.quote: the one million 18–24-year-olds across Britain who are neither in employment, education or training (NEET) are not a homogenous group

insights.claim: The UK NEET rate of 15.6% compares with 6.1% in the Netherlands, 8.6% in Ireland and 10.6% in Germany.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: The UK is a clear international outlier on youth disengagement, signalling large untapped labour supply if closed.
insights.quote: Their NEET rate of 6.1 per cent, is two-thirds lower than the UK (15.6 per cent).

insights.claim: Of the 23 OECD countries with lower NEET rates than the UK, all except the United States and New Zealand achieved this entirely through higher youth participation in education or combined education and work, not through higher employment.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Reframes the policy target from job creation to post-16 education; beneficiaries would be FE providers and skills pipelines rather than employers.
insights.quote: all but two (the United States and New Zealand) achieved this entirely by having more young people participating in education or combining education and work

insights.claim: Real-terms Further Education funding per 16–18-year-old student in England fell by 8% between 2010-11 and 2025-26, and restoring it to 2010-11 levels would cost around £1 billion.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Signals a likely spending pressure point; watch whether the Milburn Review and Treasury commit FE money.
insights.quote: real-terms funding per 16-18-year student fell by 8 per cent between 2010-11 and 2025-26

themes.theme: Redirecting the Growth and Skills Levy to under-25s

insights.claim: Employers often use the apprenticeship levy (renamed the Growth and Skills Levy) to fund high-cost, high-level courses for older, often incumbent employees rather than young people.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Levy design currently subsidises upskilling of existing staff; ringfencing would shift corporate training subsidy away from senior staff programmes.
insights.quote: employers often choose instead to use it to fund high-cost, high-level courses for older (and often incumbent) employees

insights.claim: Ringfencing Growth and Skills Levy funding for under-25s would provide a £1.5 billion boost to the courses NEETs need, and removing degree apprenticeships from levy funding would add a further £240 million.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Degree-apprenticeship providers (including universities) face funding risk if this recommendation is adopted.
insights.quote: ringfencing GSL funding for under-25s, which would provide a £1.5 billion funding boost

themes.theme: Targeted job subsidies beat employer NI tax cuts

insights.claim: Cutting employer National Insurance for under-25s, as employers have requested, would cost £5.1 billion (2026 data), or about £132,000 per additional young person helped into work.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Argues against a business-lobbied tax break; a low-value-for-money policy at a time of strained public finances.
insights.quote: costing £5.1 billion (based on 2026 data) or more pointedly, £132,000 for every additional young person helped into work

insights.claim: Targeted Youth Jobs Grants and the Jobs Guarantee cost around £36,000 per additional young person employed, and doubling both would cost about £300 million a year and help an extra 40,000 young people into work.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Cheaper, targeted schemes are the more fiscally plausible lever; watch for budget allocations to these programmes.
insights.quote: Doubling funding for both programmes would cost around £300 million a year and help an additional 40,000 young people into work.

themes.theme: Ending the 'left alone' benefit system with 'career start' support

insights.claim: The 260,000 young people receiving Universal Credit Health have no requirements to engage with support towards work, education or training.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A large, disengaged cohort is the main target for welfare reform; implies new conditionality obligations are coming.
insights.quote: The 260,000 young people currently receiving Universal Credit Health (UCH) have no requirements to engage with support

insights.claim: Rather than 'work first' conditionality pushing claimants into any available job, young benefit claimants should be required to engage with permanent, positive and personalised 'career start' employment support modelled on the Dutch approach.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Signals demand for expanded employment-support delivery (work coaches, provider contracts) rather than pure benefit cuts.
insights.quote: we need a ‘career start’ approach – permanent, positive and personalised employment support

themes.theme: Funding gap: benefit cuts cannot pay for the ambition

insights.claim: Matching average OECD spending on employment support would require at least £5bn more, and Dutch-quality support would mean more than doubling current UK spending on work coaches, training schemes and wage subsidies.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A serious NEET strategy implies multi-billion fiscal commitments competing with other priorities in a tight budget.
insights.quote: Even matching average OECD spending on those types of schemes would mean spending at least £5bn more.

insights.claim: The total benefits bill for young people is £8.1 billion, limiting how much a 'tough love' benefit cut could fund new investment in the short term, though long-run fiscal gains could be larger as caseloads fall.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Benefit cuts are an insufficient funding source; expect either new borrowing/tax or scaled-back ambition.
insights.quote: the total benefits bill for young people is £8.1 billion, so there is clearly a limit to any such hope at least in the short term

insights.claim: Receipt of Universal Credit Health and/or Personal Independence Payment currently keeps 120,000 young people out of poverty, though around one in five young PIP recipients did not experience additional costs, suggesting some savings are possible via the Timms Review.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Flags PIP as the likelier savings target and the Timms Review as the next policy catalyst.
insights.quote: around one-in-five young people currently receiving PIP did not experience additional costs
